claims.claim: A tariff is a tax (customs duty) a government imposes on imported goods, which makes imports more expensive for consumers and discourages imports while raising government revenue.
Protectionism raises the domestic price of the protected good, so domestic consumers pay more and buy less while domestic producers sell more at a higher price.

As a result of a trade barrier, consumers lose more than producers gain, so total social surplus falls; protectionism functions as an indirect subsidy from consumers to producers, and the uncaptured net loss is deadweight loss.

The three main tools for restricting trade are tariffs, import quotas (numerical limits on quantity imported), and non-tariff barriers (rules, inspections, and paperwork that raise import cost); an export subsidy instead pays domestic producers to sell abroad.
The infant-industry argument for protection is countered by the observation that temporary protection often becomes long-lasting and that many protected industries never mature.

Dumping means selling exported goods below their cost of production; the anti-dumping argument for duties is contested because cross-border predatory pricing is hard to document and cost of production is hard to measure.

Tariffs can be levied ad valorem (a percentage of value) or specific (a fixed charge per unit); a country's bound rate is a promised ceiling and its applied rate is what it actually charges, which can be lower.
Because of comparative advantage, trade raises living standards, so restricting trade forgoes gains that come from comparative advantage, specialization, and economies of scale.

In a specific-tariff example with a $100/ton tariff raising the domestic price from $500 to $600, domestic output 20 to 40 tons and consumption 100 to 80 tons, tariff revenue is $4,000, consumer-surplus loss about $9,000, producer-surplus gain about $3,000, and deadweight loss $2,000.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether tariffs and other protection are, on balance, good policy.
positions: Efficiency view: protection imposes a net deadweight loss and mainly transfers surplus from consumers to producers, so most economists favor open trade.
Protection view: infant-industry, national-security, anti-dumping, and jobs arguments raise real distributional and strategic concerns that efficiency analysis alone does not settle.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally in the lesson. The positive mechanics (price up, quantities shift, deadweight loss) are taught as settled; the normative question of whether to protect is labeled contested, naming both sides and declaring no winner, per the subject's positive-vs-normative control.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, 34.1 Protectionism: An Indirect Subsidy from Consumers to Producers
sourceRecords.notes: Supports definitions of protectionism, tariffs, import quotas, and non-tariff barriers; the mechanism by which protection raises the domestic price so producers gain and consumers pay more for less; the result that consumers lose more than producers gain, lowering social surplus (an indirect subsidy from consumers to producers); and the sugar illustration of price and quantity effects. Read via WebFetch. NC-SA source used reference-only; no prose reproduced. The lesson's numeric steel example is original, not from this page.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, 34.3 Arguments in Support of Restricting Imports
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the infant-industry, anti-dumping (with the definition of dumping as selling below cost of production), national-security, and environmental/labor arguments for protection, each with the standard economic counterargument, and the mainstream view that protection makes consumers pay more to benefit producers and forgoes gains from comparative advantage, specialization, and economies of scale. Read via WebFetch. Reference-only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Tariffs
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative source that tariffs are customs duties on merchandise imports that give a price advantage to locally produced goods and raise revenue for governments, and that bound rates are ceiling commitments while applied rates are what members actually charge (and can be lower). The ad valorem vs specific ($7 per 100 kg) distinction was corroborated via the WTO glossary through WebSearch. Main tariffs page read via WebFetch. Copyrighted; reference-only, described in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Back to Basics: International Trade — Commerce among Nations
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative primer supporting that comparative advantage means trade raises living standards for both partners, so trade restrictions forgo real gains; used to frame the efficiency case against protection and to hand off comparative-advantage theory to that topic. Located and summarized via WebSearch on imf.org; used reference-only, described in original wording.
